items.argument: Arity drops by one at every level. The full binary tree has 2^n leaves after n levels; its internal expressions still contain variables, as the known erratum clarifies.

items.claim: Constant elimination in the multilinear expansion
items.argument: Zero and unit simplifications remove zero coefficients; the empty monomial remains exactly when f(0)=1. The zero function has the empty sum represented by 0.

items.claim: Displayed three-variable polynomial calculation
items.argument: The two outer branches are 1 XOR xy and x XOR y XOR xy; multiplying the second by z gives precisely the five displayed monomials.

items.claim: Existence and uniqueness of multilinear normal form
items.argument: Induction uses the unique split P=G+xn H, recovered by evaluations at 0 and 1. Nullary base and the 2^n subset-indexed monomials are explicit.

items.claim: Boole cofactor decomposition
items.argument: The last-variable value selects exactly the corresponding cofactor; the two branches cannot simultaneously be true.

items.claim: Repeated Boole expansion produces exactly the true minterms
items.argument: The recursive split partitions all assignments. Each resulting minterm selects one assignment; its coefficient is that assignment’s function value.

items.claim: All eight minterms of the displayed four-variable truth table
items.argument: The eight original minterms correspond in order to 0000,0001,0100,0111,1100,1101,1110,1111, exactly the table’s true inputs.

items.claim: Unique full DNF and empty/nullary conventions
items.argument: Each true input forces its unique minterm. Duplicates are normalized by idempotence; empty OR=0 and empty AND=1 cover constants and n=0.

items.claim: Full CNF construction and all eight example clauses
items.argument: Each minclause excludes its unique false assignment. The eight printed clauses correspond in order to all eight zeros of (22); constants and n=0 are covered.

items.claim: General DNF/CNF indexing and literal semantics
items.argument: The indexed products/sums expand exactly as displayed; incomplete terms, empty cases and tautological/contradictory terms are distinguished. No empirical PLA performance claim is certified.

items.claim: DNF terms imply the function; first displayed witness
items.argument: T=1 forces T OR U=1. The first term in the printed three-term example selects precisely (1,0,1), where the function is true; the continuation on p54 is separate.

items.claim: All six pronouns in the implication interpretation
items.argument: With x implies y, the allowed pairs are 00,01,11. Successive pronouns y,x,x,y,y,x give possible converse, direct implication and contrapositive, respectively.

items.claim: All sixteen Pincusian operation translations
items.argument: Complement both input codes and output: D(f)(x,y)=not f(not x,not y). The complete reversed-complement table is checked row by row.

items.claim: Duality transfers every identity
items.argument: Structural induction proves t*(x)=not t(not x), with every operation dualized and constants complemented. Thus equality transfers; De Morgan and XOR/equivalence identities are explicitly paired.

items.claim: Maximum under signed Boolean coding
items.argument: The order-preserving code s=2b−1 sends maximum to OR.

items.claim: Minimum under signed Boolean coding
items.argument: The same increasing code sends minimum to AND.

items.claim: Signed negation
items.argument: Changing s to −s changes b to 1−b, hence complements the bit.

items.claim: Signed product with true=+1
items.argument: The product is +1 exactly when signs agree, so it represents equivalence.

items.claim: Signed product with true=−1
items.argument: The reversed code makes product −1 precisely for one true input, so it represents XOR.

items.claim: Majority is sign of the signed sum
items.argument: Three signs sum to ±1 or ±3, never zero; the sum’s sign equals the majority sign under either encoding.

items.claim: Every displayed NAND formula without constants
items.argument: All sixteen printed formulas are reduced through exact abbreviations and matched to their truth tables. Tree operation counts are 5,3,5,0,5,0,5,3,6,5,1,2,1,2,1,2; repeated subexpressions are counted repeatedly.

items.claim: All minimum NAND formula lengths without constants
items.argument: Root-child supports force the lower bounds. A minimal formula among XOR and equivalence cannot contain either as a child; remaining possible child pairs force five operations for both. No syntactic enumeration.

items.claim: Every displayed NAND formula with constants
items.argument: All sixteen printed formulas have the required truth tables and tree counts 0,2,3,0,3,0,5,3,4,5,1,2,1,2,1,0.

items.claim: All minimum NAND formula lengths with constants
items.argument: Classify costs zero through two and then use exact root-child support constraints. OR costs at least three; XOR/equivalence at least five by the shared minimal-formula argument; all remaining lower bounds match the witnesses.

items.claim: Minimum variable occurrences among minimum-length formulas
items.argument: Dependencies require one occurrence per essential variable. A variable occurring once in a NAND tree has fixed monotonic polarity; XOR/equivalence require each variable twice. All printed constant-allowed formulas attain these lower bounds.

items.claim: Correctness and termination of the formula-generation method
items.argument: Every optimal tree decomposes into optimal subtrees; operation and variable costs are additive. Induction over tree size proves completeness of increasing-cost generation. Explicit witnesses bound the last needed cost by six or five; the generator was not run.

items.claim: Simple transistor realizations of NAND and NOR
items.argument: In the cited CMOS switch model, series/parallel complementary pull-down/pull-up networks realize NAND and NOR with four switches. Physical performance is not certified.

items.claim: Bits encode finite information, relations and algorithm descriptions
items.argument: Inject a finite alphabet into fixed-length binary blocks; concatenation preserves distinguishability. Incidence bits encode finite relations, and finite algorithm descriptions are finite strings. No universal speed advantage or hardware prevalence claim is inferred.

items.claim: Exactly six functions without constants
items.argument: C(a,b)=not a AND b implies its right child; induction makes every term imply its rightmost variable. Supports are therefore subsets of x or y, giving exactly truth tables 0000 through 0101.

items.claim: All six witnesses have minimum length
items.argument: The printed six formulas are evaluated. Zero-cost functions are x,y, and one C-node gives only 0 and the two nonimplications; AND therefore needs two nodes and all other displayed costs are immediate minima.

items.claim: All sixteen displayed constant-allowed formulas
items.argument: Every original formula is matched to its truth table and tree cost. XOR costs five and equivalence four; subexpressions are expanded at each occurrence, never shared.

items.claim: All sixteen minimum formula lengths
items.argument: Root output is a subset of the right child. Exact support supersets force the OR/NAND bounds and a noncircular minimum-over-XOR/equivalence argument proves lower bounds five/four. Every bound matches the printed witness without formula enumeration.

items.claim: Secondary minimum variable counts
items.argument: A variable occurring once has fixed polarity determined by its unique path, so XOR/equivalence need two occurrences of each variable. All witnesses attain the dependency lower bounds; the already proved cost-generation invariant P0554 applies.

items.claim: All associative binary Boolean operations
items.argument: Eight positive operations follow from exact existing laws or immediate constant/projection semantics. Each of the other eight has an explicit three-bit witness with unequal bracketings.

items.claim: The cancellation identity implies associativity in any algebra
items.argument: From (ab)(bc)=ac derive three fully parenthesized identities with explicit substitutions, then the displayed three-step associativity proof. No associativity, finiteness or Boolean assumption is used in advance.

items.claim: Exactly six Boolean operations satisfy (xy)(yz)=xz
items.argument: The general lemma excludes all nonassociative operations. AND and OR have concrete counterexamples; constants, projections, XOR and equivalence satisfy the identity directly.

items.claim: Every term reduces to the displayed normal form
items.argument: Associativity yields words. Internal adjacent letters commute, and duplicate internal pairs cancel, while endpoints remain fixed. Sorting and cancellation terminate with a strictly increasing interior subset, or a single generator.

items.claim: Exact free-system cardinality n+2^n n^2
items.argument: An explicit algebra of separate atoms and endpoint/parity triples uses symmetric difference in multiplication. It satisfies the defining identity and distinguishes every canonical word. All triples are generated, proving the lower count and universal free-system claim, not merely an upper bound.

items.claim: The reversible two-input operations are exactly XOR and equivalence
items.argument: The necessary identity makes each column a permutation, hence f(x,y)=x XOR a_y. Equal columns are impossible, leaving x XOR y XOR c. Both directions of the required equivalence follow by cancellation for either c.

items.claim: Left distributivity as two unary endomorphism conditions
items.argument: For each fixed left input, the corresponding unary row must preserve the right operation. Identity imposes no condition, constants require S0/S1, and negation requires exactly the four self-dual binary functions.

items.claim: Complete classification of all distributive pairs
items.argument: Every one of the sixteen left truth tables is mapped to the exact intersection of its two unary preservation conditions, reproducing all seven groups in the answer with necessity and sufficiency.

items.claim: Exactly 92 ordered pairs
items.argument: The disjoint left-operation groups have sizes 3,3,2,3,2,2,1 and admissible right-set sizes 8,8,4,4,2,2,16; their products sum to 92 without enumeration.

items.claim: The full printed Schroeder condition
items.argument: Each of the three terms is exactly a failure of constant-one, constant-zero or complement preservation. Their OR is zero precisely when distributivity holds; all original negation marks are checked.

items.claim: False identity and its corrected formula
items.argument: x=y=0,z=1 is an explicit counterexample. Adding XOR z on the right gives a valid identity, proved separately for z=0 and z=1.

items.claim: Odd three-term XOR identity
items.argument: z=0 gives the original three-term XOR, while z=1 gives three ones and hence one on both sides.

items.claim: All three forms equal the not-all-equal indicator
items.argument: Each disjunction of two pairwise inequalities vanishes exactly when x=y=z. This proves the statement and both additions in the answer.

items.claim: Complete multilinear polynomial of example (22)
items.argument: The original cofactor tables g=10100011 and h=00110000 give g=1+y+w+wy+wx and h=x+wx, hence the printed seven-term polynomial. Existing uniqueness P0532 is reused.

items.claim: General parity formula for every multilinear coefficient
items.argument: Summing f(1_T) over T contained in U cancels every smaller monomial with even multiplicity, leaving a_U. The requested four-index monomial, all eight three-variable coefficients and the empty-set case are covered.

items.claim: Unique integer multilinear interpolation and the introductory example
items.argument: The weighted minterm sum gives integer coefficients and the exact vertex values. Cofactor induction proves uniqueness over integers or reals, including nullary constants. The stated polynomial for example (19) is checked by all four Hamming-weight cases.

items.claim: Complete integer polynomial of example (22)
items.argument: At w=0 the polynomial is 1−y−xz+2xyz, and at w=1 it is x. Expanding (1−w) times the first branch plus wx yields exactly all nine printed terms.

items.claim: Signed subset formula for every integer coefficient
items.argument: Boolean-lattice inversion gives a_U=sum over T contained in U of (−1)^(|U|−|T|)f(1_T). Cancellation proves it for every subset, and all eight three-variable coefficient notations are checked.

items.claim: Sharp coefficient bound with an explicit nullary-domain limit
items.argument: For nonempty U of size k, half of the 2^k signs are positive and half negative, so |a_U|≤2^(k−1). Together with |a_empty|≤1 this proves the printed maximum for n≥1. If the wording includes n=0, the constant 1 has coefficient 1 rather than at most 1/2. The positive-arity proof is complete; the literal nullary scope remains partial without a finding card.

items.claim: Parity attains the coefficient bound and has the displayed symmetric polynomial
items.argument: (1−product(1−2x_j))/2 equals parity on Boolean inputs. Expanding gives e1−2e2+4e3−...+(−2)^(n−1)en, whose top coefficient attains 2^(n−1) for every n≥1.

items.claim: Exact Hadamard component after the known erratum
items.argument: For the restricted table h on U, the integer coefficient is (−1)^k H_h(1,...,1), or exactly H_g(1,...,1) after complementing all k input coordinates. Original volume-2 equation (38) was inspected read-only; the full expansion is not confused with one unmodified transform.

items.claim: Values remain in [0,1] on the entire real cube
items.argument: All minterm weights are nonnegative and sum to one; the extension is a convex combination of Boolean values, including all boundary and nullary cases.

items.claim: Vertex order extends throughout the real cube
items.argument: G−F is a nonnegative weighted sum of the nonnegative vertex differences, so F≤G everywhere in [0,1]^n.

items.claim: Boolean monotonicity implies monotonicity of the real extension
items.argument: Each coordinate derivative is the difference of its two cofactor polynomials. Vertex monotonicity and part (d) make this nonnegative throughout the smaller cube; changing coordinates one at a time proves the full order statement.

items.claim: Independent reliability equals the integer multilinear extension
items.argument: Independence makes each state probability the corresponding minterm weight. Summing disjoint successful states gives precisely F(p), including endpoint probabilities, the verbal three-unit example and the exactly-three-working function.

items.claim: Optimal self-dual selection by complementary pairs
items.argument: Exactly one state from each complementary pair must be true. Choosing its larger probability independently is necessary and sufficient for the global optimum, with ties and endpoint probabilities explicitly covered.

items.claim: All four odds comparisons
items.argument: For interior probabilities the common product of failure probabilities cancels, yielding exactly the four printed inequalities. No monotonicity condition on the chosen function is assumed.

items.claim: The first optimum is ternary majority
items.argument: Odds 9,4,7/3 satisfy the first three inequalities and reverse the last since 9<28/3. The four true states are exactly majority, uniquely; availability is 451/500.

items.claim: The second optimum is the first projection
items.argument: Odds 4,3/2,2/3 make all four comparisons strict in the printed direction. The true states are precisely x1=1 and availability is 4/5.

items.claim: The third optimum is the complement of the third input
items.argument: Odds 4,3/2,1/9 select 000,110,010,100, exactly not x3. The original negation mark is checked and availability is 9/10.

items.claim: Exact reuse of integer-valued binomials and the binary Lucas test
items.argument: Reuse the complete V1 binomial-congruences argument: binom(t,k) is integral for every integer t and fixed k≥0; for nonnegative t,k its parity is one exactly when k’s bits are contained in t. The p=2 and input-domain assumptions are checked.

items.claim: General integer-valued polynomial representing a Boolean function modulo two
items.argument: Replace each multilinear monomial indexed by S with binom(t,sum over j in S of 2^(j−1)). The result is integral on all integers, including negative ones, and agrees modulo two on every encoded Boolean input.

items.claim: Both binomial examples and exact interpolation
items.argument: 11=1011 proves the first parity example. The displayed binomial product isolates t=11 on 0..15; its general form isolates every k on 0..2^n−1 and gives an exact integer-valued interpolation without modulo two.

items.claim: Full DNF permits XOR or ordinary addition
items.argument: Distinct complete minterms cannot simultaneously hold, so OR/XOR/sum agree, including empty cases. The ordinary DNF x OR y gives a direct counterexample to an unrestricted substitution.

items.claim: Two-level NAND form and the required n-ary convention
items.argument: De Morgan proves the two-level realization when each node is the explicitly n-ary NAND. Unary NAND is complement and nullary NAND is zero; the already proved nonassociative binary counterexample explains why unqualified binary chaining is invalid.

items.claim: Normalized terms, clauses and subcubes
items.argument: Consistent terms and nontautological clauses correspond to nonempty truth/false cubes; literal deletion frees a coordinate and primality means maximal inclusion. The precise normalization domain is explicit, including empty terms and clauses.

items.claim: Complete three-variable prime example
items.argument: The four true vertices form a path with exactly the three displayed maximal edges; explicit false witnesses exclude every further literal deletion. Both original terms expand exactly as printed.

items.claim: All five primes of the four-variable example
items.argument: The complete eight-edge true-set graph has four bridges and one square, so its maximal cubes are exactly the five listed terms. The known correction before (30) is incorporated.

items.claim: Both redundant prime examples and their exact minima
items.argument: Private true points force two terms/four literals in the first example and four terms/eleven literals in the second. Extending arbitrary consistent terms to primes transfers the lower bounds to every DNF.

items.claim: Completeness of disjunctive and conjunctive prime forms
items.argument: Every true minterm extends finitely to a maximal true cube, and false cubes give the dual statement. Constants and nullary cases use explicit empty-family conventions.

items.claim: Every DNF term and CNF clause share a literal
items.argument: For a consistent term T and nontautological clause C, T implies C exactly when they share a literal; otherwise their simultaneous truth/false requirements are consistent and contradict the two equivalent normal forms.

items.claim: All four clause/implicant equivalences
items.argument: The common-literal criterion is proved both ways for all implicants, all prime implicants, and every term of any fixed normalized DNF. Full minterms and the prime cover supply the converses.

items.claim: Complete list of maximal false cubes
items.argument: All eight false-set edges, its isolated vertex and pendant edge, and its two squares are listed. These exhaust the four maximal false cubes and exclude larger cubes.

items.claim: Prime CNF and minimum of four clauses/eleven literals
items.argument: Each of the four clauses has a private false point. Every clause extends its false cube to a prime, so those points force all four distinct primes and at least eleven literals, attained by the printed CNF.

items.claim: Primes of a conjunction
items.argument: Extend a maximal cube of f AND g separately to maximal cubes of f and g. Their nonempty intersection still lies in the conjunction and contains the original maximal cube, hence equals it. Constant and vacuous cases are explicit.

items.claim: Equivalent monotonicity definitions
items.argument: Increasing one coordinate at a time proves equivalence between the single-bit condition and coordinatewise order preservation.

items.claim: Monotone iff representable with AND and OR
items.argument: Both cofactors are monotone and ordered; the cofactor expansion becomes g OR h x_n. Induction from constants proves existence, and simplification removes constants for a nonconstant function. Composition proves the converse.

items.claim: Prime implicants of monotone functions contain only positive literals
items.argument: Deleting a negative literal remains an implicant: any newly admitted point is above an old point. This contradicts primality.

items.claim: The complete prime DNF is shortest for a monotone function
items.argument: Each positive prime has its private characteristic-vector witness. Extending arbitrary DNF terms to primes cannot increase length, and all primes are forced. Term-count optimality is distinguished from uniqueness of syntactic minimum formulas.

items.claim: Positive antichains characterize monotone prime forms
items.argument: A positive antichain term cannot be shortened because its characteristic vector would then contain a strictly smaller original term. Any additional prime must contain an original term, so primality forces equality.

items.claim: Unate extension and printed example
items.argument: Complementing fixed coordinates is a cube automorphism preserving inclusion, maximal primes, literal counts and private witnesses. It transfers Theorem Q back; the printed NOT x OR y becomes x OR y.

items.claim: Satisfiable iff nonzero iff has a consistent implicant
items.argument: A true point gives a minterm and a prime extension, while a consistent implicant contains a true point. This also fixes the intended normalization domain of exercise18.

items.claim: SAT NP-completeness as an explicit external input
items.argument: Cook's official Clay problem description, pp4–5, supplies the exact formula-SAT and reduction statement. Its complete computation-simulation proof is not reconstructed.

items.claim: Polynomial-time SAT question and current open status
items.argument: Polynomial means one algorithm with fixed exponent in formula length. SAT is in NP by assignment evaluation; with the explicit external completeness input, polynomial SAT is equivalent to P=NP. Official Clay status checked on 2026-11-06 remains unsolved.

items.claim: Exact input representation of minimum-DNF hardness
items.argument: For arbitrary formula input, a polynomial minimum-DNF algorithm would decide SAT by inspecting its output; the reduction and output-size premise are explicit. This does not establish the same hardness for truth-table or DNF input, which the local text does not fix.

items.claim: Complete prime-generation algorithm
items.argument: The general generator now has full correctness, completeness, tag and stack proofs P0654–P0659. The remaining limit is the runtime interpretation documented as candidate C0004/P0660; the corrected control-flow version has a separate bound P0661.

items.claim: Necessary and sufficient monotonicity conditions
items.argument: The two cofactors must be monotone and ordered; the pointwise order is exactly g AND h=0. Both directions, constants and an example showing h itself need not be monotone are explicit.

items.claim: The complete prime CNF
items.argument: Minimal transversals of the three positive terms are exactly {x}, {v,y}, {v,z}, {w,z}; the case split proves completeness as well as primality.

items.claim: General distributive construction of monotone prime CNF
items.argument: The precise dual of Corollary Q proves the positive-antichain characterization. Finite recursive distribution and absorption terminate and produce all prime clauses; no polynomial cost is claimed.

items.claim: Complete count and length recurrences for alternating trees
items.argument: Disjoint leaf supports make both the union at OR and Cartesian product at AND into positive antichains. This proves completeness, distinctness and both count/length recurrences from k=0.

items.claim: Closed formulas and every index in the k=6 example
items.argument: Parity induction proves all four formulas. Fourteen independent choices t_a,t_ab,t_abc give the exact eight-leaf product indexed by a t_a b t_ab c t_abc, a bijection yielding 2^14=4^7 primes.

items.claim: Minimal path vertex covers and the complete counting recurrence
items.argument: The final-vertex cases are bijections with smaller minimal covers, not merely upper bounds. All covers for n=2,3,4 are listed and the empty-product n=1 limit is separated.

items.claim: Lexicographic shelling of all path-cover primes
items.argument: For earlier A<B, the first difference i yields j=i+1 in A minus B. Replacing i by j and minimizing preserves the prefix and gives an earlier cover C with C minus B={j}; thus every earlier A meets the shadow of B. Increasing bit-vector order is explicit.

items.claim: Exact Perrin expression
items.argument: The linear combination (7P_n+10P_(n+1)+P_(n+2))/23 obeys the proved cover recurrence and has all three required initial values. Original P3/P4/P5 and the explicit backward P2 extension fix the domain.

items.claim: Exhaustive assignment count and formula semantics
items.argument: All 2^n assignments suffice when each is evaluated; 2^30=1,073,741,824. Assignment count is separated from evaluation work, and the modeling statement is treated as the meaning of f(x)=1.

items.claim: Random truth-table satisfiability and fewer than two expected trials
items.argument: For m=2^n independent fair entries, Pr(SAT)=1−2^(−m). Testing distinct points until success or exhaustion gives E T=2(1−2^(−m)); conditional on SAT it is 2−m/(2^m−1). The asymptotic and nullary interpretations are explicit.

items.claim: Shortest unsatisfiable 3CNF and the eight-clause lower bound
items.argument: One nonempty clause is satisfiable and two opposite repeated literals attain the unrestricted minimum. With three distinct variables per clause, a union bound gives success probability at least 1−m/8 without assuming independent clauses, hence at least eight are needed.

items.claim: Every clause and every seven-clause subformula
items.argument: The eight false cubes are listed with both vertices; they partition all sixteen assignments. Removing any clause leaves exactly its two points and fixes three coordinates. The known permutation C8,C1,…,C7 preserves the claim and changes first seven to last seven.

items.claim: Four 3CNF clauses encode every binary gate
items.argument: For each input pair only its matching clause constrains the output, forcing exactly the operation value. This proves all sixteen gates at once, checks the printed AND example and includes aliased children and constant operations. The known 2015 replacement x^p=[x=p] is the explicit reindexing (p,q) to (1−p,1−q) of the same four clauses; the amended example is also covered.

items.claim: Whole-tree reduction, exact clause count and costs
items.argument: For corrected N>0, bottom-up induction gives a unique extension for each original assignment. The root clause yields the pointwise existential equivalence. There are exactly N fresh variables and 4N+1 unsimplified clauses, O(N) word operations/output and polynomial binary encoding.

items.claim: Precise polynomial comparison of SAT and 3SAT
items.argument: The verified gate construction is a polynomial reduction from formula-SAT, while 3CNF is already a formula. With explicit external input P0614 and direct certificate checking this proves 3SAT completeness without assuming P differs from NP.

items.claim: Prime-family domain and all constant representations
items.argument: Both set families are antichains without duplicates. Empty families and singleton empty members encode the four constant cases; irrelevant coordinates may be restored arbitrarily.

items.claim: Disjoint-member witness
items.argument: The characteristic vector of a DNF member disjoint from a CNF clause gives g=1,f=0, including empty members. Failure of this test establishes g≤f.

items.claim: Both unequal-support witnesses
items.argument: A variable present in only one family yields an explicit witness after deleting it from the relevant member or complementing that construction. The antichain condition excludes all other members; both directions are proved.

items.claim: Both excessive-size witnesses
items.argument: Selecting one point from every required intersection uses fewer points than the oversized member. The resulting characteristic vector, or its complement, satisfies f and falsifies g; all prime assumptions are explicit.

items.claim: Efficient conditional-count witness
items.argument: The sum counts incidences of bad assignments. Prefix counts preserve S<2^r; choosing a child below half yields a witness after n steps. Exact integer representation and a polynomial bit-cost implementation are given, including n=0.

items.claim: Correct cofactors and preserved prime invariant
items.argument: All four reduced families follow directly from fixing x_k. Absorption preserves each cofactor and restores a positive antichain, hence its full prime form. Cardinalities never increase and empty members are normalized.

items.claim: All terminal cases
items.argument: After the witness tests fail, product zero gives equal constants and product one gives the same singleton variable. All empty-family combinations are checked explicitly.

items.claim: Recursive correctness and termination
items.argument: Both child products strictly decrease. A child witness extends to the correct parent branch; two equal cofactor pairs imply equality. Induction proves return validity and finite termination.

items.claim: Short member and the branching-ratio bound
items.argument: The failed measure test gives m≤lg N. Every opposite member intersects a shortest member, so one coordinate occurs in at least a 1/m fraction, proving the selected ratio is at most 1−1/lg N.

items.claim: A fixed recurrence majorizes every recursive call
items.argument: Using fixed rho=1−1/lg N0 throughout the whole recursion, both child products are at most v−1 and one is at most floor(rho v). This proves the printed A recurrence without confusing varying local ratios.

items.claim: Quasipolynomial call bound with boundary cases
items.argument: Unfolding B=A+1 gives the printed factor bound; the floor(rho v)=0 case is handled separately. At most O(log² N0) shrink steps and polynomial factors yield N0 raised to O(log² N0); N0≤2 is terminal.

items.claim: Per-node polynomial work and input-size meaning
items.argument: Intersection tests, conditional counts, absorption and frequency selection have explicit polynomial implementations. Passing support/size tests bounds active variables and incidence by the family product. Initial input reading is charged to actual encoded length.

items.claim: Duality equivalence and complete prime-generation addendum
items.argument: Duality exchanges prime clauses and terms. Starting from a=0≤g*, a difference yields a new minimal true point after at most n evaluations, preserving the invariant. Each iteration adds a distinct prime and finite completion returns g*, with output size explicitly charged.

items.claim: Refined Fredman–Khachiyan bound as a precise external input
items.argument: The original paper, p620 Theorem1, gives N raised to 4 chi(N)+O(1), chi^chi=N. The domain and encoding assumptions on p619 were read and the asymptotic relation checked. The refined algorithm itself is not independently reconstructed.

items.claim: Current open status and conditional complexity interpretation
items.argument: A primary October 2026 paper still states output-polynomial dualization is open. Only that status is used. Quasipolynomial solvability would transfer to SAT under polynomial NP-completeness reductions; this is a conditional implication, not a proof that completeness is impossible.

items.claim: Every clause and prime term of the cover example
items.argument: The eight true points give the eight printed incidence clauses, reducing exactly to y1 y4 y5 (y2 OR y3). The complete two-prime list follows from the positive antichain theorem; existing optimum proofs are reused.

items.claim: Exact positive-implicant correspondence and the unqualified wording
items.argument: Selected prime covers correspond bijectively to positive implicants of g, and irredundant covers to prime implicants. The answer says every implicant without a positive restriction; two explicit consistent terms with and without NOT y3 have the same selected cover. The implicit domain remains qualified; no finding card is created.

items.claim: Every shortest DNF yields a prime cover term
items.argument: A nonprime term can lose a literal and a redundant term can be removed, so a shortest literal/operator expression is a prime irredundant cover. The claim is distinguished from minimizing only the number of terms, and constants are explicit.

items.claim: Buddy-scan orientation and lower-bound invariant
items.argument: The lower endpoint has bit j zero and target v+2^j. Two increasing pointers maintain the first not-yet-excluded target candidate; exact matches, misses and exhaustion all preserve completeness and output order.

items.claim: Safety of the large-mismatch jump
items.argument: A mismatch above bit j places the upper pointer in a later 2^(j+1) block. Every skipped zero-bit lower endpoint would require a partner in the missing upper half of the original block, proving the jump safe.

items.claim: Termination, O(m) time and optional steps
items.argument: Both pointers only advance, with O(m) total advances and iterations. Empty/singleton input and the highest bit are explicit. Removing B3 or B5 retains the standard invariant and linear bound.

items.claim: Cube encoding, every buddy example and tag maximality
items.argument: The pair (a,b) uniquely encodes each nonempty cube. All three named buddies are checked. A contained buddy gives a larger cube, and every larger cube supplies a buddy, proving tag zero iff maximal.

items.claim: Exact initialization and tag transfer
items.argument: Each point receives each buddy bit at most once. A merged cube has an l-buddy exactly when both halves do, so the new tag is the intersection with bit j cleared; subtraction is valid because j is present.

items.claim: Stack layout, sorted lists and safe writes
items.argument: Header/start indices, empty lists and pop addresses are explicit. New data never overwrite the scanned parent or its header. Input order and the lower buddy endpoint preserve sorted canonical b values.

items.claim: 109(a): the majorization order and its complement anti-isomorphism
items.argument: Prefix differences recover the unique word. Complement replaces A_k by k-A_k, reversing every inequality, including k=0 and the empty word.

items.claim: 109(b): greatest lower bound, closure and computation
items.argument: The coordinatewise minimum of prefix sums has increments zero or one. Its universal lower-bound property is proved, and one streaming pass computes the word in O(n) word operations and O(1) auxiliary words.

items.claim: 109(c): least upper bound, closure and computation
items.argument: The coordinatewise maximum has increments zero or one and satisfies the full universal upper-bound property. The complement-of-meet expression follows from the anti-isomorphism.

items.claim: 109(d): both distributive laws
items.argument: Both scalar min/max distributivities are proved by ordering the two arguments. Applying them to each prefix and recovering differences proves both lattice identities.

items.claim: 109(d) addition: arbitrary fixed mixed radices
items.argument: For positive integer radices m_j, prefix minima and maxima have increments between zero and m_j-1. This establishes domain closure, universal properties and distributivity, including radix one.

items.claim: 109(e): exhaustive cover characterization
items.argument: Deleting a final one or swapping adjacent 10 to 01 lowers one prefix by one, so gives a cover. Conversely, the first strict prefix and the following run of ones produce one such move remaining above any lower word, excluding all other covers.

items.claim: 109(f): rank and every saturated path length
items.argument: The sum of all prefixes equals sum((n-i+1)*a_i). Every cover lowers it exactly one; the constructive cover argument guarantees a path to zero. Thus every requested path has precisely the stated length.

items.claim: 109 and Fig.8: every printed vertex, edge and rank
items.argument: All 32 labels and all 48 edges are listed and compared with the enlarged original. The 16 final-bit deletions and 32 adjacent swaps are exactly the general cover characterization; every displayed level matches the rank.

items.claim: 109(g): the leading-one recurrence
items.argument: Every word above 1 alpha must begin with one; deleting that bit is a bijection with words above alpha. Hence m(1 alpha)=m(alpha).

items.claim: 109(g): the leading-zero recurrence and zero-word boundary
items.argument: Split dominators of 0 alpha by their first bit. The leading-one case requires B_k>=A_k-1, exactly dominance over alpha with its first one removed. The no-one and empty-word cases are explicit.

items.claim: 109(h): the exact central binomial count
items.argument: A first-crossing reflection bijects bad paths with j down-steps to all paths with j-1 down-steps. The counts telescope to binomial(n,floor(n/2)); the inverse map and n=0 are included.

items.argument: Coordinatewise inclusion implies every prefix inequality, so regularity directly implies monotonicity. The empty-coordinate case is included.

items.claim: 110(b): sorted signed weights do not imply regularity

items.argument: The proved cover characterization reduces the claim to adding the final bit and moving a one left. The score increments are w_n and w_j-w_(j+1), both nonnegative.

items.claim: 110(c): ordered weights imply ordered Chow components
items.argument: Pairing inputs differing only in two adjacent coordinates expresses s_j-s_(j+1) as a sum of nonnegative differences. The argument does not need a nonnegative last weight.

items.argument: Eight true boundary supports receive positive multipliers (1,12,3,7,7,11,16,2). Their total is 59 and every variable has weighted incidence 30, so summing necessary inequalities yields sum(w)>=59. The printed vector attains it.

items.claim: 110 addition: two actual optima with ordered Chow components
items.argument: Swapping the unequal weights 6 and 7 preserves the function by proved symmetry and gives another optimum of total 59. The swapped vector is sorted, so part (c) proves ordered Chow components for the original unsorted optimum.

items.claim: 110 final addition: strict Chow order forces strict weight order
items.argument: If the weights were ordered oppositely or equal, the same paired-input argument would force the opposite weak Chow inequality. This proves the strict implication for general threshold representations.

items.argument: The unique optimal vector from proof-091 has exactly one repeated pair. Every variable automorphism must preserve that unique optimum; swapping the pair is indeed an automorphism. The stabilizer therefore has size two, giving 9!/2=181440 distinct relabellings without enumeration. Whether the book implicitly counts canonical types remains a separate P1114 interpretation limit.

items.claim: 111(a): regularity, including all ties
items.argument: Majorization cannot decrease H because its weights are sorted and nonnegative. On a zero-score tie, a true x has x1=1 and every larger y has y1=1. Thus the chosen optimum is regular and is a valid coterie.

items.claim: 111(b): complete minimal-true-point optimality test
items.argument: Every true point lies above a minimal true point. The printed test g(y)=1 proves f<=g and hence equality by self-duality. The exact test H(y)>=0 also accepts all optimal tie choices; a strict failure loses probability. Arithmetic cost for a supplied list of t points is O(nt), excluding list generation and bit costs.

items.claim: 111(b) addition: every printed minimal point
items.argument: All seven sorted weight forms, their complete prime families and all twelve minimal majorization points are tabulated. The domination and incomparability checks establish completeness; at most twelve function-value tests suffice to find an optimum among the seven.

items.claim: 111(c): coordinatewise monotonicity of optimal availability
items.argument: Each availability polynomial is monotone by the precisely reused P0585. The maximum over the finite nonempty class of monotone self-dual functions is therefore also monotone.

Hence its availability is unchanged when the bad probabilities are restored, attaining the monotonic upper bound.

items.claim: 111(c): fixed-circle intersection bound

items.claim: 111(c): the full uniform intersection bound by double counting

items.argument: Monotonicity bounds the heterogeneous optimum by the equal-p1 optimum, which the layer proof bounds by p1. Projection x1 attains p1, proving a global optimum over all coteries.
